p.x:
Last week, I bought a T-shirt online for the first time. First, I did a search for "blue T-shirt". There were hundreds! I compared the prices and chose one from a seller with good reviews. Other buyers said it was good quality.
I put the T-shirt in my basket and made the payment with my mum's card. Three days later, a package arrived at our house.
But there was a problem. It was the wrong size! It was too small. I sent it back, and the seller sent me a bigger one. Now it fits perfectly.

Online shopping has become part of everyday life in Thailand. Online marketplaces sell almost everything, from clothes and phones to food and furniture. You simply add items to your cart, go to the checkout and choose how to pay. Some people use a debit card or scan a QR code, others pay with an e-wallet, and many still prefer cash on delivery, paying the driver when the parcel arrives.
There are many ways to save money. Shops offer a coupon or a promo code, and many orders come with free shipping. If not, you may pay a small delivery fee. Every month, there is a big flash sale, when prices drop for just a few hours. Shoppers often add products to their wishlist and wait for the sale. Sometimes, a popular item is out of stock, but you can pre-order it.
Of course, online shopping has disadvantages. Because buying is so easy, many people make an impulse buy and later regret it. Some even call themselves a shopaholic! And all those parcels create waste: boxes, plastic bags and bubble wrap. On the bright side, parcels arrive right on your doorstep, and watching unboxing videos has become a popular hobby.

E-commerce has transformed the retail industry. In Southeast Asia, online sales have grown rapidly over the past decade, driven by cheap smartphones, fast internet and efficient logistics. In major cities, same-day delivery is now common: an order placed in the morning can be dispatched within an hour and arrive by evening. For those who are not at home, parcels can be sent to a pick-up point, such as a convenience store, or to a locker at a train station. Cross-border shipping has also made it easy to buy directly from factories overseas.
Behind the convenience lies sophisticated technology. Online stores collect data on everything customers search for, click on and buy. This information is used to create personalised recommendations and adverts designed to encourage further purchases. A newer trend is live-stream shopping, in which sellers show products in real time and viewers buy instantly.
Critics warn that these techniques exploit human psychology. Limited-time offers, countdown timers and messages such as "only two left" create a sense of urgency that makes consumers more likely to overspend. Many people splurge during major sales events and later struggle to pay their credit card bills.
Shoppers are advised to take simple precautions: set a budget, wait a day before making large purchases, and only enter payment details on secure websites.
